column1: # Bare deref of a Function-typed PARAM
# (design/FUNCTION-VALUE-SCOPE.0.md §11 rule 3, §12.4).
# RULED 2026-08-15 (maintainer): A BARE NAME IS A CALL; `/v` is how you ask for
# the value. Arity discrimination was considered and explicitly rejected.
# Under that rule the INTERPRETER is correct in both rows below and the COMPILER
# is wrong — it lowers the param to a unit local (RegisterLocal) and reads it as
# a value, so it neither applies nor raises:
#   [f]  arity 0     correct: APPLY   interp: applies (7)  compiler: Function
#   [c]  arity >=1   correct: RAISE   interp: raises       compiler: Function
# The `expected` column is therefore the DECIDED answer, not merely the
# interpreter's — they now coincide. Graduation = the compiler treats a bare
# Function-bound name as a call, at which point these rows move to the main
# corpus.
# The Function SLOT is NOT at fault and never was: stepWord's TFunction
# intercept binds the argument as a reference, driven by
# hasPendingForwardExpectingFunction reading SigArgType off the pending forward.
# A SEPARATE bug, tracked in §12.4 and not represented here because it is an
# interpreter fault rather than a divergence the compiler can graduate: `/v`
# fails to park a 0-arg fn bound to a PARAM. `typeof nought/v` at module level
# is Function on both engines and `[c/v]` at arity >=1 is Function on both, but
# `[f/v]` at arity 0 yields 7 on the interpreter. The documented way to pass a
# function as a value silently does the opposite in that one shape.
def nought fn [[] [Integer] [7]] def grab fn [[f:Function] [Any] [f]] typeof (grab nought)
column3: arity-0 Function param read bare: the interpreter APPLIES it (7 -> Integer), the compiler yields the Function

column1: def dbl fn [[n:Integer] [Integer] [n mul 2]] def hold fn [[c:Function] [Any] [c]] typeof (hold dbl)
column3: arity-1 Function param read bare with no argument: the interpreter RAISES, the compiler yields the Function
